fields.name: Entropion
fields.definition: Eyelid margin turns inward, so lashes and skin rub against the surface of the eye.
fields.etiology: Aging; cicatricial (burn, surgery, trauma, chronic inflammation, scar); congenital.
fields.risk_factors: Aging; scarring from burn, surgery, trauma or chronic inflammation; congenital.
fields.pathology: Lashes pushed onto the globe (trichiasis) cause irritation and corneal abrasion/potential corneal damage.
fields.clinical: Foreign body sensation, irritation, pain; conjunctival injection; inward-turned lid margin with lashes on the globe.
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; slit lamp exam to check for corneal involvement.
fields.treatment: Preservative-free artificial tears by day, lubricating ointment at night; tape lid into place; surgery is definitive.

fields.name: Ectropion
fields.definition: Lower eyelid sags and turns outward, exposing the inner surface of the lid.
fields.etiology: Aging; cicatricial (burn, surgery, trauma, chronic inflammation, scar); congenital; facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) palsy (ectropion only).
fields.risk_factors: Aging; scarring; congenital; facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) palsy.
fields.pathology: Everted lid margin leaves the eye exposed, causing exposure keratopathy.
fields.clinical: Tearing; conjunctival injection; outward-turned lid margin.
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; slit lamp exam to check for corneal involvement.
fields.treatment: Preservative-free artificial tears by day, lubricating ointment at night; tape exposed lid into place; surgery is definitive.

fields.name: Dermatochalasis
fields.definition: Excess, loose, sagging skin of the upper or lower eyelids.
fields.etiology: Aging.
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Lid "heaviness", "looking through lashes", lid friction with blinking; bilateral excess flaps/folds of lid skin.
fields.diagnosis: Examine visual fields for deficits.
fields.treatment: Blepharoplasty; often covered by insurance if a visual field defect is present.

fields.name: Xanthelasma
fields.definition: Harmless, soft, yellowish cholesterol deposit under the skin on or around the eyelids.
fields.etiology: Metabolic disorders with increased serum lipids.
fields.risk_factors: Elevated serum lipids (dyslipidemia), though many patients have normal lipid levels.
fields.pathology: Cholesterol deposit under the eyelid skin.
fields.clinical: Typically asymptomatic; oval yellowish plaques on the eyelids.
fields.diagnosis: Serum lipid profile and cardiovascular risk assessment; diabetes labs (fasting plasma glucose, hemoglobin A1C); liver function labs.
fields.treatment: Treat the underlying metabolic issue; local cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen), laser ablation, chemical peel or surgical excision; recurrences common despite effective local treatment.

fields.name: Blepharitis / meibomitis
fields.definition: Blepharitis: common, non-contagious inflammation of the eyelid margins. Meibomitis: inflammation of the meibomian (lid-margin oil) glands.
fields.etiology: Rosacea, seborrheic dermatitis, colonization with Staphylococcus aureus.
fields.pathology: Chronic lid-margin and meibomian gland inflammation with thickened lipid secretion; controlled rather than cured.
fields.clinical: Burning, dryness, grittiness, itching, foreign body sensation, tearing; crusting/scaling at lash bases (collarettes), red swollen lid margins, thick toothpaste-like meibomian secretion, frothy tear film; rosacea or seborrheic skin findings.
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Lid hygiene (over-the-counter lid scrub); no improvement after 2 weeks: topical, then oral antibiotics; refer to ophthalmology if not improved after several weeks.

fields.name: Chalazion
fields.definition: Sterile obstruction of a meibomian gland producing a nontender eyelid nodule.
fields.etiology: Sterile meibomian gland obstruction.
fields.pathology: Sterile obstruction of a meibomian gland.
fields.clinical: Focal eyelid swelling over days to weeks; visible/palpable subcutaneous lid nodule that is nontender.
fields.diagnosis: Refer recurrent chalazia or those persisting more than 2 to 3 months to rule out sebaceous carcinoma.
fields.treatment: Warm compresses, gentle massage (improvement may take months); refer to ophthalmology for steroid injection or curettage if no spontaneous resolution; recurrent with rosacea needs ophthalmology.

fields.name: Hordeolum (also: stye)
fields.definition: Acute inflammation of a meibomian gland (internal hordeolum) or of the glands of Zeis or Moll (external hordeolum).
fields.etiology: Usually staphylococcal infection.
fields.pathology: Acute, usually staphylococcal, inflammation of a meibomian gland (internal) or Zeis/Moll gland (external).
fields.clinical: Eyelid pain, redness and swelling developing over 24 hours/overnight; visible/palpable subcutaneous lid nodule that is tender.
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Warm compresses, gentle massage; refer to ophthalmology for incision and drainage if persistent (no improvement in 2 weeks); with associated pre-septal cellulitis, systemic antibiotics as for pre-septal cellulitis.

fields.name: Dacryoadenitis
fields.definition: Inflammation of the lacrimal gland (the tear-producing gland above the eye).
fields.etiology: Inflammatory (most common); bacterial (rare); viral (usually bilateral).
fields.pathology: Inflamed, hyperemic palpebral lobe of the lacrimal gland.
fields.clinical: Unilateral pain, redness, swelling over the lateral one-third of the upper lid; tearing or discharge; possible ipsilateral preauricular lymphadenopathy, temporal conjunctival injection, fever, leukocytosis.
fields.diagnosis: CT (computed tomography) of orbits and paranasal sinuses with contrast, especially if severe, orbital findings, chronic, atypical, suspected abscess/mass or not improving.
fields.treatment: As-needed acetaminophen; unclear cause: empiric oral antibiotics for 24 hours then reassess; inflammatory: oral corticosteroids (after excluding infection; respond within 48 hours); viral: cool compresses; monitor for orbital involvement.

fields.name: Dacryocystitis
fields.definition: Infection or inflammation of the lacrimal (tear) sac, usually from a blocked tear duct.
fields.etiology: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction.
fields.pathology: Obstructed nasolacrimal duct leads to infection/inflammation of the lacrimal sac.
fields.clinical: Red, painful, tense swelling over the lacrimal sac at the medial lower lid (below the medial canthal tendon); tearing, fever; mucoid/purulent discharge expressible from the lower punctum. Mass above the tendon: suspect lacrimal sac tumor.
fields.diagnosis: Mainly clinical; CT (computed tomography) of orbits and sinuses with contrast if orbital extension, abscess, trauma, mass or atypical disease.
fields.treatment: Mild, afebrile: oral antibiotics for 10 days; febrile/ill: admit, intravenous antibiotics 48 to 72 hours then oral to 10 to 14 days with prompt ophthalmology consult; warm compresses; consider abscess drainage; later probing/irrigation or surgery.

fields.name: Pinguecula
fields.definition: Non-cancerous yellowish or white deposit on the conjunctiva that does not involve the cornea.
fields.etiology: Chronic exposure to sunlight and wind.
fields.pathology: Conjunctival deposit confined to the conjunctiva, not crossing the limbus onto the cornea ("penguins can't fly").
fields.clinical: Irritation, redness nasally and/or temporally, tearing; classic appearance almost always at 3 or 9 o'clock.
fields.diagnosis: Clinical appearance; slit lamp exam of the adjacent cornea if referred.
fields.treatment: Protect eyes from sun, dust, wind; artificial tears; non-urgent referral to ophthalmology if growth or vision impairment. Conservative care will not make it resolve.

fields.name: Pterygium (also: surfer's eye)
fields.definition: Non-cancerous, raised, wedge-shaped fleshy conjunctival growth that extends onto the cornea.
fields.etiology: Chronic exposure to sunlight and wind.
fields.pathology: Triangular, insect-wing-shaped fleshy conjunctival growth invading the cornea ("pterodactyls fly into the cornea").
fields.clinical: Irritation, redness nasally and/or temporally, tearing; sometimes decreased vision; almost always at 3 or 9 o'clock.
fields.diagnosis: Clinical appearance; slit lamp exam to evaluate integrity of the adjacent cornea; differential: conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia (more fan-like).
fields.treatment: Protect eyes from sun, dust, wind; artificial tears; non-urgent referral if growth or vision impairment; surgery if growing into the cornea and distorting vision.

fields.name: Subconjunctival hemorrhage (atraumatic)
fields.definition: Harmless broken blood vessel producing a bright red patch of blood underneath the conjunctiva.
fields.etiology: Valsalva, bleeding disorder, antiplatelet/anticoagulant medications, hypertension.
fields.pathology: Bleeding beneath the conjunctiva.
fields.clinical: Red eye, often asymptomatic unless chemosis is present; blood under the conjunctiva. Differential: 360-degree traumatic hemorrhage, hyphema.
fields.diagnosis: History is key; ocular exam; check blood pressure if no explanation; recurrent: medication review, blood pressure, targeted hematologic evaluation (may need hematology if no culprit medication).
fields.treatment: Reassurance; usually resolves spontaneously within 2 to 4 weeks (uncomplicated often about 1 to 2 weeks, larger ones longer); artificial tears for mild irritation; treat underlying bleeding disorder or hypertension.

fields.name: Chemosis
fields.definition: Swelling (edema) of the conjunctiva; more a sign/presentation than a diagnosis.
fields.etiology: Allergy, infection, thyroid eye disease, angioedema, trauma, orbital cellulitis, impaired orbital venous drainage.
fields.pathology: Nonspecific conjunctival edema from eye irritation.
fields.clinical: Swollen conjunctiva; nonspecific sign of eye irritation.
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Urgent when accompanied by proptosis, restricted eye movement, reduced vision or an afferent pupillary defect.

fields.name: Acute allergic conjunctivitis
fields.definition: Non-infectious conjunctivitis: allergic inflammation of the conjunctiva ("pink eye").
fields.etiology: Reaction to a systemic allergen.
fields.pathology: Allergic conjunctival inflammation forming papillae (red at surface, paler at base).
fields.clinical: Itchy, bilateral red eyes; swollen lids; watery/stringy discharge; preserved vision; chemosis, papillae, no preauricular node.
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Avoid allergen; cool compresses, artificial tears, topical H1 (histamine-1) blocker with or without mast cell stabilizer (olopatadine does both), systemic H1 blocker; refer to ophthalmology if not relieved. Uncomplicated conjunctivitis: routine disposition.

fields.name: Acute viral conjunctivitis
fields.definition: Infectious inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by a virus.
fields.etiology: Most common: adenovirus; isolated ocular vs systemic infection; may follow or accompany an upper respiratory infection.
fields.risk_factors: Concomitant or preceding upper respiratory infection.
fields.pathology: Viral conjunctival inflammation forming follicles (pale at surface, redder at base).
fields.clinical: Diffusely red eye, profuse watery discharge, swollen tight lids but no pain; bilateral (often starts in one eye); inferior follicles; tender preauricular nodes.
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Cool compresses, artificial tears; contagious precautions, hand hygiene; refer to ophthalmology if lasting more than 3 weeks or photophobia/decreased vision (uncomplicated: routine disposition). Self-limiting; worse over first week, resolves in 2 to 3 weeks.

fields.name: Autoimmune conjunctivitis
fields.definition: Conjunctival inflammation associated with systemic autoimmune disease.
fields.etiology: Many autoimmune disorders, often already identified: ocular mucous membrane pemphigoid, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, Sjögren disease, graft-versus-host disease.
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Diffuse, often recurrent/chronic conjunctival hyperemia; minimal/no pain, no discharge; systemic complaints (malaise, fever, fatigue).
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Routine referral to ophthalmology; ocular response depends on the underlying autoimmune disorder.

fields.name: Acute bacterial conjunctivitis
fields.definition: Infectious inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by bacteria.
fields.etiology: Bacterial infection.
fields.epidemiology: Seen in immunocompromised, elderly and pediatric populations and contact lens wearers.
fields.pathology: Bacterial conjunctival inflammation forming papillae.
fields.clinical: Diffuse red eye, thick yellow or white purulent discharge, possible soreness; often unilateral; florid hyperemia, chemosis, papillae; usually no preauricular node.
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; contact lens wearers need corneal assessment for microbial keratitis.
fields.treatment: Immunocompetent adult: topical broad-spectrum antibiotic (fluoroquinolone); hand hygiene. Referral: uncomplicated = routine; urgent ("immediate ophthalmology involvement") if immunocompromised, contact lens wearer, recent surgery, foreign body, corneal opacity/keratitis or no improvement in 24 hours.

fields.name: Gonococcal conjunctivitis (neonatal)
fields.definition: Bacterial conjunctivitis from gonococcus; the major concern in neonates.
fields.etiology: Gonococcal bacterial infection.
fields.pathology: Risk if untreated: corneal perforation.
fields.clinical: Severe purulent discharge with a palpable preauricular node.
fields.diagnosis: Cultures/Gram stain; testing for chlamydia and disseminated infection.
fields.treatment: Emergent referral and hospitalization; immediate systemic ceftriaxone (intravenous/intramuscular, single dose); specialty consultation.

fields.name: Adult chlamydial conjunctivitis (also: adult inclusion conjunctivitis)
fields.definition: Chronic (more than 4 weeks) conjunctivitis from Chlamydia trachomatis in adults.
fields.etiology: Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes D to K by direct inoculation with infected genital secretions.
fields.pathology: Chlamydial conjunctival inflammation forming follicles; preauricular node enlargement.
fields.clinical: Chronic hyperemia of the lower palpebral conjunctiva, stringy mucoid discharge, unilateral (sometimes bilateral), lasting a month or more and unresponsive to topical medications; follicles.
fields.diagnosis: Conjunctival NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) or DFA (direct fluorescent antibody) stain of conjunctival scraping confirms; diagnosis often delayed.
fields.treatment: Oral doxycycline for 7 days (avoid sun, full glass of water, stay upright, separate from antacids/minerals); evaluate for other sexually transmitted infections; notify partners. Resolves in weeks without permanent damage.

fields.name: Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis
fields.definition: Chlamydial conjunctivitis in newborns.
fields.etiology: Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes D to K by direct inoculation with infected genital secretions.
fields.epidemiology: Neonates; those born to mothers with cervical infection may also have or develop pneumonia.
fields.risk_factors: Direct inoculation with infected genital secretions (maternal cervical infection).
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Conjunctivitis; may also have or develop pneumonia/pneumonitis.
fields.diagnosis: Assess for pneumonia.
fields.treatment: Erythromycin for 14 days (monitor infants under 6 weeks for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis); azithromycin alternative; often treated in hospital because of concomitant pneumonia.

fields.name: Trachoma
fields.definition: Chlamydial eye infection; leading infectious cause of blindness worldwide.
fields.etiology: Recurrent infection with Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes A, B, C; highly infectious.
fields.epidemiology: Transmitted rapidly in areas of poor hygiene; leading infectious cause of blindness worldwide.
fields.pathology: Repeated infection: conjunctival inflammation, then eyelid scarring, then entropion, then trichiasis (lashes rubbing the eye), then blindness.
fields.clinical: Most active cases asymptomatic; if symptomatic: red eye, foreign body sensation, purulent discharge, follicles (especially upper lid).
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Mass drug administration of single-dose oral azithromycin where prevalence is 5% or more; usually curative, reinfection common without better hygiene; trichiasis requires surgery.

fields.name: Episcleritis
fields.definition: Common, generally harmless inflammation of the episclera (thin layer of tissue between the white of the eye and its clear outer covering; deep subconjunctival tissue)
fields.etiology: Often idiopathic; often no systemic association
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Acute-onset mild pain and focal, often sectoral redness; no discharge or photophobia; episcleral vessels move slightly with a cotton-tip applicator (after anesthesia); may recur in same or other eye
fields.diagnosis: Phenylephrine 2.5% test: one drop in affected eye, wait 15 min, episcleral vessels should blanch
fields.treatment: Artificial tears + oral NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug), taken with food; refer to ophthalmology if no response within 2 days; usually self-limited, resolves over 2–3 weeks

fields.name: Scleritis
fields.definition: Painful, serious inflammation of the sclera (tough white outer layer of the eye)
fields.etiology: Often a systemic autoimmune condition
fields.pathology: Inflammation of scleral, episcleral and conjunctival vessels; scleral thinning lets the choroid show through (bluish, violaceous area); sclera at risk for perforation, greatest in necrotizing disease
fields.clinical: Severe boring eye pain, worse at night, radiating to face/periorbital region, may wake patient; pain with eye movement; diffuse conjunctival injection; violaceous hue of sclera; scleral vessels do NOT move with cotton-tip applicator (after anesthesia)
fields.diagnosis: Slit lamp exam and ophthalmoscopy (fundoscopy) by ophthalmology; work-up for underlying systemic condition
fields.treatment: Referral urgency, two stated: urgent referral to ophthalmology (scleritis management) and same day (red-eye referral timing); systemic corticosteroids or other immune-modulating agents (noninfectious anterior: often systemic NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) first); may need surgical patch; less pain = first sign of response

fields.name: Pre-septal (periorbital) cellulitis (also: periorbital cellulitis)
fields.definition: Bacterial infection of the eyelid and skin around the eye, in front of the orbital septum
fields.etiology: Direct extension from bacterial sinus, skin or dental infection; in diabetic, elderly or immunocompromised consider fungus (aspergillosis, mucormycosis)
fields.risk_factors: Diabetic, elderly, or immunocompromised: consider fungal cause
fields.pathology: Preseptal soft-tissue inflammation on CT (computed tomography)
fields.clinical: Periocular pain, fever/chills, warmth; diffuse balloon-like edema, erythema, tenderness of lids and periorbital tissue; variable conjunctival injection; eye itself is white; vision, pupils and eye movements normal
fields.diagnosis: CT (computed tomography) of orbits and paranasal sinuses with contrast (mild, clearly preseptal disease may be managed clinically without routine CT); complete eye exam with fundoscopy; Gram stain/culture of drainage; CBC (complete blood count) with differential; blood cultures
fields.treatment: Mild: outpatient oral antibiotics 10–14 days aimed at Staphylococcus (with or without MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus)) and Streptococcus; moderate-severe (toxic), poor compliance, age 5 or younger, or failing oral: admit + IV (intravenous) antibiotics 48–72 hours, then oral at least 1 week

fields.name: Post-septal (orbital) cellulitis (also: orbital cellulitis)
fields.definition: Dangerous bacterial infection of the tissues inside the eye socket, behind the orbital septum
fields.etiology: Direct extension from bacterial sinus (e.g. ethmoiditis), skin or dental infection; in diabetic, elderly or immunocompromised consider fungus (aspergillosis, mucormycosis)
fields.risk_factors: Diabetic, elderly, or immunocompromised: consider fungal cause
fields.pathology: Inflammatory stranding of retrobulbar (intraconal and extraconal) soft tissue with proptosis and tenting of the posterior globe on CT (computed tomography); untreated may spread intracranially: meningitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis
fields.clinical: Periocular pain, fever/chills, lid edema/erythema PLUS painful, decreased extraocular movement, reduced vision, diplopia, proptosis, significant conjunctival injection (eye itself red), possible afferent pupillary defect
fields.diagnosis: CT (computed tomography) of orbits and paranasal sinuses with contrast; complete eye exam with fundoscopy; Gram stain/culture of drainage; CBC (complete blood count) with differential; blood cultures
fields.treatment: Referral urgency, two stated: emergent (red-eye referral timing) and urgent ophthalmology/ENT (ear, nose, throat) involvement (cellulitis management); all cases: hospitalization + broad-spectrum IV (intravenous) antibiotics 48–72 hours, then oral at least 1 week; ENT, oral maxillofacial surgery and/or infectious disease consults

fields.name: Keratitis (also: microbial keratitis)
fields.definition: Inflammation of the cornea (clear, dome-shaped window covering the front of the eye)
fields.etiology: Bacterial, viral, fungal infection; parasitic rare (Acanthamoeba, a free-living amoeba in soil, dust, water)
fields.epidemiology: Acanthamoeba keratitis occurs primarily in contact lens wearers with poor lens hygiene (e.g. rinsing lens with tap water)
fields.risk_factors: Corneal trauma, dry eyes, contact lens overwear (overnight wear increases risk), topical ocular corticosteroid therapy
fields.pathology: Ciliary flush from anterior ciliary artery branches signals corneal inflammation; undertreated: corneal scarring or perforation → endophthalmitis
fields.clinical: Eye pain, foreign body sensation, tearing, photophobia, redness at edge of cornea, blurred vision; corneal opacity/haziness, “broken up” corneal light reflex, ciliary flush; Acanthamoeba: classic corneal ring infiltrate
fields.diagnosis: Slit-lamp exam with fluorescein (epithelial defect, white infiltrate); culture/smear for large, central, deep, atypical or unresponsive ulcers (preserve lenses/case)
fields.treatment: Referral urgency, two stated: urgent, within 24 hours (keratitis management) and same day (red-eye referral timing); treat underlying cause to prevent scarring; remove contacts, do not patch; no take-home topical anesthetic or corticosteroid

fields.name: Herpes simplex keratitis (also: dendritic keratitis)
fields.definition: Herpetic keratitis from herpes simplex virus, showing a true dendrite on the cornea
fields.etiology: HSV-1 (herpes simplex virus type 1) much more common in the eye than HSV-2
fields.pathology: Recurrent disease can cause stromal scarring, neurotrophic keratopathy, glaucoma, need for corneal transplant, permanent visual loss
fields.clinical: Primary HSV-1 infection often not clinically apparent; facial vesicles lack dermatomal distribution and may not respect midline (only 10% of primary dermatitis bilateral); recurrences common
fields.diagnosis: Fluorescein with cobalt blue light: true dendrite (“tree branching”, stained central bed, unstained raised edges, terminal end bulbs) = pathognomonic; slit-lamp + dilated fundoscopy by ophthalmology
fields.treatment: Refer to ophthalmology; oral antivirals (acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir) × 10 days; NO topical glucocorticoids by primary care with active epithelial disease, leave to ophthalmology

fields.name: Herpes zoster keratitis (also: herpes zoster ophthalmicus (ocular involvement); pseudodendritic keratitis)
fields.definition: Herpetic keratitis from herpes zoster with pseudodendrites on the cornea
fields.etiology: Herpes zoster virus
fields.epidemiology: Patients often older; rare in children; also seen in immunosuppressed (e.g. HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), cancer)
fields.risk_factors: Older age; immunosuppression; Hutchinson sign (tip of nose involved) = higher risk of ocular involvement
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Pain/paresthesias of affected skin, may follow headache, fever, malaise; dermatomal vesicles (most often V1 (first trigeminal division)) respecting midline, unilateral, often spares lower lid; rash may precede eye involvement by days to months; postherpetic neuralgia
fields.diagnosis: Fluorescein with cobalt blue light: pseudodendrites lacking tree-branch pattern, raised edges and terminal end bulbs; slit-lamp + dilated fundoscopy by ophthalmology
fields.treatment: Refer to ophthalmology (ocular herpes zoster ophthalmicus: same day); oral antivirals × 10 days (ideally within 72 hours of rash), IV (intravenous) acyclovir if immunocompromised/severe; steroid drops per ophthalmology; retinitis/choroiditis/optic neuritis: corticosteroids + IV acyclovir; zoster vaccine prevention

fields.name: Corneal ulcer
fields.definition: Open sore on the cornea (clear front surface of the eye)
fields.etiology: Eye infection, corneal abrasion, severe dry eyes, eyelid closure problems, autoimmune diseases (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis: peripheral ulceration)
fields.pathology: Corneal defect; heals with scar (may calcify); ciliary flush from anterior ciliary artery branches signals corneal inflammation
fields.clinical: Painful eye, reluctance/resistance to opening eye (photophobia, foreign body sensation), tearing, blurred vision, red eye; ciliary flush; white spot with surrounding corneal irregularity
fields.diagnosis: Slit lamp and fluorescein exam; swab for culture of central and/or large ulcers
fields.treatment: Referral urgency, two stated: emergent referral to ophthalmology (corneal ulcer management) and same day (red-eye referral timing); start broad-spectrum topical agent (4th-generation fluoroquinolone); steroid drops only per ophthalmology; next-day follow-up; severe/unresponsive may need corneal transplant

fields.name: Anterior uveitis (also: iritis; iridocyclitis)
fields.definition: Inflammation of the front of the uvea: iris (iritis) or iris and ciliary body (iridocyclitis)
fields.etiology: Idiopathic, autoimmune; may be infectious
fields.pathology: White cells in anterior chamber, keratic precipitates (white blood cell deposits on posterior surface of cornea); iris adheres to lens (posterior synechiae) giving irregular pupil
fields.clinical: Eye pain, redness at edge of cornea, photophobia, vision often preserved; consensual photophobia (pain in affected eye when light shone in other eye); ciliary flush; variable IOP (intraocular pressure); irregular pupil
fields.diagnosis: Slit lamp exam (cells, “snowstorm” in anterior chamber, flare) and dilated fundoscopy; systemic evaluation if recurrent or signs of systemic autoimmune disease
fields.treatment: Referral urgency, two stated: urgent, within 24 hours (uveitis management; delay risks vision loss) and same day (red-eye referral timing); infectious: treat organism; noninfectious: often topical corticosteroids; acute cases respond in days–weeks, chronic slowly

fields.name: Posterior uveitis (also: choroiditis; retinitis)
fields.definition: Inflammation of the back of the eye: the choroid (vascular middle layer) and frequently the retina
fields.etiology: Idiopathic, autoimmune, infectious (toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus)
fields.pathology: Cells in posterior vitreous, vitreous haze, inflammation of retina or choroid; develops more slowly than anterior uveitis, may last years
fields.clinical: Blurred vision, floaters, scotomas, metamorphopsia; no pain if isolated posterior uveitis; may be acute and rapidly vision-threatening
fields.diagnosis: Slit lamp exam and dilated fundoscopy; possibly fluorescein angiography (active vs inactive lesions)
fields.treatment: Refer to ophthalmology (long-term follow-up); by cause, like anterior uveitis, but not responsive to topical treatment: may need intraocular corticosteroid injection; exclude infection before immunosuppression

fields.name: Nystagmus
fields.definition: Involuntary, biphasic, rhythmic, tremor-like oscillating movement of the eyes.
fields.etiology: Congenital (infantile or latent) or acquired; upbeat nystagmus is always abnormal (cerebellar or medullary lesion), less commonly drug intoxication; pendular type often congenital or after prolonged bilateral blindness beginning in childhood.
fields.epidemiology: Most common form is horizontal jerk nystagmus.
fields.pathology: Jerk: slow drift then fast beat, named for the fast-phase direction (vertical, horizontal, torsional), worse gazing toward the fast phase; horizontal types: physiologic gaze-evoked, infantile, spasmus nutans, latent. Pendular: both phases equal velocity and amplitude, mostly horizontal.
fields.clinical: Usually symptomatic unless acquired before age 8: vertigo (often primary symptom, common with vestibular problems); oscillopsia (environment seems to move back and forth); blurred vision; abnormal compensatory head positioning.
fields.diagnosis: Refer/work up: infants and young children with nystagmus; nystagmus acquired in adolescence or adulthood; concerning adult nystagmus (upbeat, monocular/asymmetric, non-physiologic horizontal). Complete ophthalmic exam, then initial imaging, then labs if relevant.
fields.treatment: Referral to ophthalmology; the underlying etiology must be addressed.

fields.name: Opioid overdose (pupillary constriction)
fields.definition: Overdose of opioids, which act as parasympathomimetics on the pupil.
fields.etiology: Excess opioid intake.
fields.pathology: Parasympathomimetic effect on the pupillary constriction pathway causes miosis.
fields.clinical: Decreased mental status, respiratory depression (under 12/min), decreased tidal volume, pupillary constriction; mental status and breathing are what matter clinically.
fields.diagnosis: Monitor pupil size alongside breathing: pupils may re-constrict before respiratory depression returns, signaling need for another dose.
fields.treatment: Naloxone (preferably intravenous; intranasal available over the counter); lasts about 2 hours, so repeat if respiratory depression and coma return; can continue until pupils dilate.

fields.name: Anisocoria (also: asymmetric pupils; physiologic (benign) anisocoria)
fields.definition: Unequal pupil size; pupils should be unequal only when the efferent pathways are not working properly.
fields.etiology: Most commonly physiologic. Small pupil abnormal: ocular condition preventing dilation, miotic drops (pilocarpine), sympathetic dysfunction (Horner). Large pupil abnormal: pharmacologic mydriasis (anticholinergics, sympathomimetics), trauma including prior eye surgery, Adie tonic pupil, cranial nerve III palsy.
fields.risk_factors: Ocular trauma; topical medications; toxin and drug exposure (atropine, ipratropium, scopolamine, glycopyrrolate, clonidine, phenylephrine, epinephrine).
fields.pathology: Efferent limb is bilateral, so both pupils normally receive the same command. Anticholinergic pupil is usually 8 mm or more and nonreactive; sympathomimetic pupil only 1-2 mm larger than baseline.
fields.clinical: Physiologic: usually under 0.4 mm, equal in light and dark, no dilation lag, usually persistent, may switch sides. Small pupil abnormal if it dilates poorly in dim light; large pupil abnormal if it constricts poorly to light.
fields.diagnosis: History (trauma, old photographs, topical drugs, toxins, neuro signs); compare pupils in light and dark. More in dark: apraclonidine (small pupil dilates = Horner). More in light: 0.1% pilocarpine constricts Adie pupil; no constriction to 1% pilocarpine = pharmacologic.
fields.treatment: Physiologic anisocoria can be normal; note and document the difference so the cause can be worked out.

fields.name: Relative afferent pupillary defect (also: Marcus Gunn pupil)
fields.definition: Pupil sign indicating an afferent defect, usually at the level of the retina or optic nerve.
fields.etiology: Lesion of the afferent limb of the pupillary reflex (retina or cranial nerve II), i.e. the pre-chiasmal visual pathway.
fields.pathology: Diminished perception of light in the affected eye, so moving light from the normal eye to the affected eye makes both pupils dilate.
fields.clinical: Light in affected eye: no direct or consensual response; light in normal eye: both constrict; swinging light back to the affected eye: both pupils dilate at the same rate. Lid normal.
fields.diagnosis: Pupil exam moving a bright light from the normal to the affected eye. Differential: optic nerve lesion (glaucoma, optic neuritis/multiple sclerosis), retinal detachment, macular degeneration, CRVO (central retinal vein occlusion).
fields.treatment: Determined by the underlying cause.

fields.name: Horner syndrome (also: oculo-sympathetic paresis)
fields.definition: Acquired condition following damage to the sympathetic nerve supply of the eye.
fields.etiology: Often idiopathic. 1st-order: brainstem stroke/tumor, spinal cord lesion above T1. 2nd-order: Pancoast tumor (superior pulmonary sulcus), thyroid cancer. 3rd-order: carotid dissection, cavernous sinus thrombosis.
fields.risk_factors: Trauma (e.g. brachial plexus injury, carotid dissection); reported after COVID-19 with intubation/mechanical ventilation.
fields.pathology: Loss of the 3-neuron sympathetic pathway (hypothalamus, ciliospinal center of Budge C8-T2, superior cervical ganglion, along carotid) to the pupil dilator, facial sweat glands and Muller muscle.
fields.clinical: [[★ Classic triad: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis]] (anhidrosis may be absent depending on lesion site). Hallmark: [[★ dilation lag]] (anisocoria most evident 4-5 s after dimming lights). Normal levator function; usually unilateral.
fields.diagnosis: [[★ Dilute apraclonidine drops]]: no effect on normal pupil, dilate the Horner pupil in most patients. Cocaine drops are an alternative (less sensitive, costly, special storage). Carotid dissection may add focal neurologic complaints.
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Argyll Robertson pupil
fields.definition: Bilateral miosis with light-near dissociation: pupils do not constrict to light but quickly constrict with near accommodation.
fields.etiology: Classically tertiary syphilis; also diabetes mellitus, chronic alcohol use, neurosarcoidosis, multiple sclerosis, encephalitis.
fields.pathology: Exact mechanism unknown; suspected dorsal midbrain (pretectal) lesion interrupts the light reflex, while the near pathway skips that portion ([[★ basis of light-near dissociation]]).
fields.clinical: Bilateral small, irregular pupils; weak or absent light response not improved by dark adaptation; normal or brisk near response; syphilis patients may have tabes dorsalis (posterior column involvement, sensory ataxia).
fields.diagnosis: Pupils slowly dilate with atropine drops; syphilis workup may be indicated.
fields.treatment: No treatment for the pupil itself; treat the underlying cause (syphilis: intramuscular penicillin G).

fields.name: Adie tonic pupil (also: tonic pupil; Holmes-Adie syndrome)
fields.definition: Dilated pupil with poor light reaction and slow, tonic constriction and re-dilation to near effort.
fields.etiology: Inflammation (infection vs autoimmune) damaging the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves.
fields.pathology: Parasympathetic damage followed by aberrant reinnervation; pupil becomes supersensitive to cholinergic drops.
fields.clinical: Mydriasis, poor light reaction, slow near constriction then slow re-dilation; often asymptomatic or photophobia/blurring; sector paralysis on slit lamp; reduced corneal sensation; often absent Achilles/patellar reflexes; no ptosis or eye movement weakness.
fields.diagnosis: Dilute pilocarpine 0.1%: no effect on normal pupil, constricts the Adie pupil in most patients (unless acute phase); slit lamp; esthesiometer for corneal sensation.
fields.treatment: Idiopathic Adie syndrome is largely benign: reassurance. Over time the pupil becomes smaller ("little old Adie").

fields.name: Cranial nerve III (oculomotor) palsy (also: third nerve palsy)
fields.definition: Peripheral palsy of the oculomotor nerve (levator palpebrae, superior/inferior/medial rectus, inferior oblique, pupillary sphincter).
fields.etiology: Most common: microvascular disease (diabetes mellitus, hypertension). Most dreaded: compression by enlarging aneurysm, usually posterior communicating artery. Other: severe head trauma, migraine, uncal herniation.
fields.risk_factors: Diabetes mellitus; hypertension; severe head trauma (skull fracture and/or loss of consciousness).
fields.pathology: Levator palpebrae inactivated (ptosis); sphincter pupillae tone lost (mydriasis); unopposed superior oblique and lateral rectus pull eye down and out.
fields.clinical: Ptosis, mydriasis, eye "down and out"; binocular horizontal, vertical, or oblique diplopia; reduced levator function, usually unilateral.
fields.diagnosis: Classify complete vs incomplete and [[★ pupil-involved vs pupil-spared]]. Pupil involved: immediate (STAT) CTA (computed tomography angiography) head/MRA (magnetic resonance angiography) brain. Pupil-sparing: reassurance and imaging, but not urgently.
fields.treatment: By etiology. Traumatic: observe about 6 months before corrective treatment; patch one eye for diplopia. Microvascular: good prognosis, improves within weeks, resolves by 3 months. Aneurysm pre-rupture: often endovascular coiling.
fields.mortality: Aneurysm threatens rupture within hours or days; rupture is a cerebrovascular emergency.

fields.name: Cranial nerve IV (trochlear) palsy (also: fourth nerve palsy)
fields.definition: Peripheral palsy of the trochlear nerve, which supplies the superior oblique (intorts and depresses the eye); peripheral lesion gives ipsilateral deficits.
fields.etiology: Isolated palsy most commonly congenital (even in adults); acquired: trauma (even mild), microvascular disease (diabetes mellitus, hypertension).
fields.pathology: Only nerve arising from the dorsal brainstem and crossing; with superior oblique weak, the inferior oblique is unopposed in medial gaze.
fields.clinical: Binocular vertical diplopia; deficit most apparent on adduction; compensatory head tilt to the opposite side improves hypertropia, ipsilateral tilt worsens it.
fields.diagnosis: Isolated atraumatic palsy: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) brain with and without contrast; hemoglobin A1C if risk factors and no known diabetes.
fields.treatment: Traumatic: observe about 6 months before corrective treatment; patch one eye for diplopia meanwhile. Congenital: patching in children (especially under 5) under an ophthalmologist. Microvascular: resolves by 3 months.

fields.name: Cranial nerve VI (abducens) palsy (also: sixth nerve palsy)
fields.definition: Peripheral palsy of the abducens nerve, which supplies the lateral rectus (abducts the eye).
fields.etiology: Children: most commonly intracranial tumors (brainstem, posterior fossa). Adults: most commonly microvascular disease (diabetes mellitus, hypertension); also major trauma (skull base fracture).
fields.risk_factors: Diabetes mellitus; hypertension; skull base fracture.
fields.pathology: Lateral rectus weakness impairs abduction.
fields.clinical: Binocular horizontal diplopia.
fields.diagnosis: Isolated atraumatic palsy: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) brain with and without contrast; hemoglobin A1C if risk factors and no known diabetes.
fields.treatment: Traumatic: observe about 6 months before corrective treatment; patch one eye for diplopia meanwhile. Congenital: patching in children (especially under 5) under an ophthalmologist. Microvascular: improves within weeks, resolves by 3 months.

fields.name: Ptosis (also: blepharoptosis)
fields.definition: Drooping of the upper eyelid from a congenital or acquired abnormality of the muscles that elevate the eyelid.
fields.etiology: Cranial nerve III palsy, Horner syndrome, myasthenia gravis, myotonic dystrophy, pseudoptosis (dermatochalasis), mechanical (infection, inflammation, lid tumor), botulinum toxin injection, infectious botulism.
fields.risk_factors: Botulinum toxin injection of the eyelid or upper face; food or wound botulism exposure.
fields.pathology: Lid elevators: levator palpebrae superioris (cranial nerve III) and sympathetic Muller muscle (extra 1-2 mm); orbicularis oculi (cranial nerve VII) closes the lids.
fields.clinical: Clues: cranial nerve III (reduced levator, mydriasis, eye movement deficit); Horner (normal levator, miosis); myasthenia gravis (variable through the day, fatigable, diplopia); botulism (bilateral palsies, symmetric descending weakness).
fields.diagnosis: Assess levator function, laterality, pupil, eye movements and variability; myotonic dystrophy also has temporalis/sternocleidomastoid/distal weakness, cataracts, cardiac conduction issues, long hollow-cheeked face.
fields.treatment: Directed at the cause; botulinum toxin ptosis usually resolves in 3-4 weeks.

conditions.name: Pre- and post-chiasmal lesions (visual field defects)

fields.name: Pre- and post-chiasmal lesions (visual field defects)
fields.definition: Lesions along the visual pathway producing characteristic visual field defects depending on location.
fields.etiology: End-stage glaucoma (constricted field); optic neuritis in multiple sclerosis or macular degeneration (central scotoma); pituitary tumor (bitemporal hemianopia); stroke (homonymous hemianopia).
fields.pathology: Pre-chiasm (optic nerve): single-eye loss. Chiasm: bitemporal hemianopia. Post-chiasm (tract, radiation, cortex): contralateral homonymous hemianopia; optic radiation lesions can give quadrantanopia; cortex may spare the macula.
fields.clinical: Constricted field (bilateral sometimes signifies hysteria), central scotoma, total monocular blindness, bitemporal hemianopia, homonymous hemianopia, superior quadrantanopia, macular-sparing hemianopia.
fields.diagnosis: Thorough history and physical; labs and imaging (CT (computed tomography) head or MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) brain) if indicated.
fields.treatment: Ophthalmology referral; specialist referral as appropriate (neurology, vascular surgery, neurosurgery).

fields.name: Amaurosis fugax (also: fleeting blindness)
fields.definition: Transient, painless monocular vision loss lasting a few seconds to minutes; a group of disorders with benign to grave neurologic or ophthalmologic implications
fields.etiology: Retinal emboli of carotid (TIA, transient ischemic attack) or cardiac origin; retinal vascular spasm; also migraine or retinal artery occlusion
fields.risk_factors: Older age; diabetes; hypertension; atherosclerosis; cardiac valve disease; intravenous drug use; sickle cell; coagulation disorders; Raynaud phenomenon
fields.pathology: Blockage in the blood vessels that supply the retina causes retinal ischemia
fields.clinical: Transient "curtain" descending over the vision of one eye (less often ascending); mild blurring or fogging to complete blackness; part or all of the visual field; painless
fields.diagnosis: History: one or both eyes (cover each eye), duration, pain, exact symptoms; carotid Doppler if carotid source suspected; echocardiogram if cardiac source; MRA (magnetic resonance angiography) of all arteries for emboli
fields.treatment: Treat the underlying cause; aspirin and clopidogrel to reduce stroke risk; carotid endarterectomy for carotid emboli; calcium channel blockers for Raynaud/vasospasm; early evaluation reduces vision loss (~85% fully recover, the rest progress to central retinal artery occlusion)

fields.name: Acute angle-closure glaucoma (also: acute closed-angle glaucoma)
fields.definition: Emergency: the iris blocks the drainage angle and intraocular pressure rises dramatically; can cause permanent blindness without prompt treatment
fields.etiology: Severe angle occlusion by the iris; obstruction may be secondary to tumor, scarring, or other mechanical causes
fields.epidemiology: Much less common than chronic open-angle glaucoma
fields.risk_factors: Systemic anticholinergics (e.g. atropine); nebulized bronchodilators; history of anterior uveitis; lens dislocation; optic neuropathy; African American race
fields.pathology: Closed angle: iris blocks outflow through the trabecular meshwork, so fluid builds up behind the iris and intraocular pressure rises
fields.clinical: Severe, sudden eye pain; decreased vision; colored halos around lights; headache, nausea, and vomiting common
fields.diagnosis: Dilated (fixed) pupil; hazy cornea; bilateral narrow or occluded angle; tonometry or gonioscopy shows intraocular pressure 40–80 mmHg
fields.treatment: Topical pilocarpine or topical beta-blocker (timolol); IV (intravenous) acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor), then mannitol or isosorbide; definitive: laser peripheral iridotomy 1–2 days after onset

fields.name: Chronic open-angle glaucoma (also: primary open-angle glaucoma)
fields.definition: Chronic, idiopathic optic nerve damage with an open angle and progressive peripheral visual field loss
fields.etiology: Idiopathic; abnormal trabecular meshwork/canal of Schlemm secondary to aging
fields.epidemiology: Much more common than acute angle-closure; over 90% of glaucoma is primary open-angle
fields.risk_factors: African American race; Hispanic ethnicity; adults over 40 and increasing age; diabetes; family history; hypertension; myopia
fields.pathology: Aging trabecular meshwork next to the canal of Schlemm becomes blocked → optic nerve damage and visual field loss, with or without elevated intraocular pressure; optic nerve cupping (widened, deepened cup from lost nerve fibers)
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic in most; may have persistently elevated bilateral intraocular pressure; gradual peripheral vision loss → "tunnel vision" → complete blindness
fields.diagnosis: Unobstructed open angle with optic nerve defects: increased cup-to-disc ratio, rim pitting/thinning, bayoneting (narrow angulations of vessels), splinter hemorrhages; visual field defects; intraocular pressure normal or high on tonometry/gonioscopy
fields.treatment: Lower intraocular pressure; first-line drops: latanoprost, tafluprost, timolol (beta-blocker); if refractory/advanced: laser trabeculoplasty, then trabeculectomy with iridectomy

fields.name: Optic neuritis
fields.definition: Inflammatory condition that damages the optic nerve
fields.etiology: Inflammation from multiple sclerosis, autoimmune disorders, postviral, or idiopathic
fields.pathology: Inflammatory, demyelinating damage to the optic nerve; recurrence carries a greater risk of developing multiple sclerosis
fields.clinical: Unilateral vision loss over hours to days; painful eye movement; RAPD (relative afferent pupillary defect; Marcus Gunn pupil); central vision and color vision loss; disc often normal-appearing; spontaneous recovery (near-normal vision at 1 year)
fields.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis from history and exam; full ophthalmic (slit lamp, dilated fundoscopy, color vision) and neurologic exam; MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of brain and orbits with and without contrast (optic nerve enhancement; periventricular T2 FLAIR (fluid-attenuated inversion recovery) hyperintensities); may need labs
fields.treatment: Refer to ophthalmology; corticosteroids may quicken visual recovery and delay onset of multiple sclerosis; 2 or more demyelinating lesions on MRI → refer to neurology/neuro-ophthalmology

fields.name: Retinal detachment
fields.definition: Serious emergency in which the light-sensitive retina pulls away from its normal position; rhegmatogenous, traction, or serous/exudative types
fields.etiology: Commonly follows a retinal tear or hole
fields.risk_factors: Myopia; trauma; cataract extraction; diabetes; tumor; connective tissue diseases; family history
fields.pathology: Age-related shrinkage of the vitreous humor causes traction on the retina
fields.clinical: New flashes and floaters (retinal tears); gray/black peripheral shadow, a "curtain or dark cloud" that may cover the whole field in days; sudden vision loss if the macula is involved; changes with head position
fields.diagnosis: Direct and dilated ophthalmoscopy: elevated gray retina with folds, pigmented well-demarcated detachment, orange crescent-shaped tears; ultrasound determines type and is more sensitive than fundoscopy
fields.treatment: Emergency: refer immediately; surgical repair urgently or within a week by type: laser photocoagulation, cryotherapy, pneumatic retinopexy, vitrectomy, scleral buckle

fields.name: Central retinal vein occlusion (also: CRVO)
fields.definition: Blockage of the main retinal vein that prevents blood from draining, causing sudden blurry vision or vision loss
fields.etiology: Occlusion of the central retinal vein by a thrombus
fields.epidemiology: More common than central retinal artery occlusion
fields.risk_factors: Hypertension; diabetes; hyperlipidemia; Raynaud phenomenon; age over 50; hypercoagulable disorders; giant cell arteritis; endocarditis; atrial myxoma; obesity
fields.pathology: Thrombus blocks venous drainage of the entire retina; neovascularization occurs weeks to months later
fields.clinical: Sudden, painless vision loss, sometimes gradual over days to a week; more severe than branch occlusion
fields.diagnosis: Disc swelling, venous dilation, cotton wool spots, retinal hemorrhages: "blood and thunder" fundus; confirm with color fundus photography and fluorescein angiography; evaluate for underlying disorders
fields.treatment: Urgent referral to ophthalmologist to restore blood flow

fields.name: Branch retinal vein occlusion (also: BRVO)
fields.definition: Blockage of a smaller side-branch retinal vein, affecting part of the eye
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Occludes a branch vein rather than the main trunk, so only part of the retina is affected
fields.clinical: Vision loss limited to part of the eye; less severe than central retinal vein occlusion
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Central retinal artery occlusion (also: CRAO)
fields.definition: Emergency that acts like a stroke in the eye, causing sudden, painless vision loss in one eye
fields.etiology: Arteriosclerosis; atherosclerosis; carotid or cardiac emboli
fields.epidemiology: Less common than central retinal vein occlusion
fields.risk_factors: Hypertension; diabetes; hyperlipidemia; Raynaud phenomenon; old age; hypercoagulable disorders; giant cell arteritis; endocarditis; atrial myxoma; obesity; atrial fibrillation
fields.pathology: Blocked central retinal artery: [[★ irreversible retinal damage may occur after 90 minutes]]; [[★ risk of stroke increases at onset of the occlusion]]; neovascularization weeks to months later
fields.clinical: Painless, profound vision loss over seconds; acuity counting fingers to light perception; temporal "island" of vision; [[★ pupil slow to direct light but brisk when the other eye is illuminated]]
fields.diagnosis: Pale retinal swelling with cherry-red spot at the fovea; blocked arteries, segmented venous blood, emboli; color fundus photography and fluorescein angiography show absent perfusion
fields.treatment: Prompt treatment: high-concentration inhaled oxygen and digital massage over the eyelid; IV (intravenous) acetazolamide to lower intraocular pressure; anterior chamber paracentesis; thrombolytic into the ophthalmic artery within 8 hours

fields.name: Branch retinal artery occlusion (also: BRAO)
fields.definition: Sudden, painless blockage of a smaller branch retinal artery in one eye
fields.etiology: Embolus or clot
fields.pathology: Blocks a branch vessel rather than the main arterial trunk, so ischemia is localized
fields.clinical: Sudden, painless, partial, localized vision loss in one eye (vs severe, widespread loss in central occlusion)
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Papilledema
fields.definition: Swelling of the optic disc caused by increased intracranial pressure
fields.etiology: Tumor; trauma; intracranial infection; hemorrhage; vitamin A toxicity
fields.pathology: Raised intracranial pressure swells the optic disc; acute: hemorrhages, cotton wool spots; chronic: elevated disc, blurred margins; atrophic: optic nerve axons die
fields.clinical: Non-specific vision changes (flickering, blurry, double vision); signs of raised intracranial pressure: nausea, vomiting, headache
fields.diagnosis: Ophthalmoscopy: engorged retinal veins, swollen disc, ± hemorrhages; lumbar puncture: raised opening pressure confirms it; MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) and/or CT (computed tomography) of the head to rule out mass lesion
fields.treatment: Treat the underlying disorder

fields.name: Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (also: NAION)
fields.definition: Sudden loss of blood flow to the front of the optic nerve (optic disc) causing rapid, painless vision loss; the non-arteritic type
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Small, crowded optic disc ("disc at risk"); hypertension; diabetes; high cholesterol; sleep apnea
fields.pathology: Optic disc ischemia; optic nerve edema resolves within 8 weeks, leaving atrophy
fields.clinical: Sudden, painless loss of side or central vision; swollen, pale optic nerve head; usually one eye first, the other at risk; mild visual improvement in some over months
fields.diagnosis: Diagnosis of exclusion: same workup as arteritic to exclude giant cell arteritis; medical evaluation (hypertension, diabetes, anemia); neuroimaging if unclear
fields.treatment: Observation and cardiovascular risk factor modification; consider avoiding bedtime antihypertensives (nocturnal hypotension); counsel on risk to the other eye

fields.name: Arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (also: AAION; giant cell (temporal) arteritis)
fields.definition: Sudden loss of blood flow to the front of the optic nerve from giant cell arteritis; medical emergency to prevent vision loss in the other eye
fields.etiology: Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis), an inflammation of blood vessels
fields.pathology: Arteritic inflammation cuts blood flow to the optic disc; biopsy shows thickening of the media and endothelium
fields.clinical: Sudden, painless vision loss; swollen, pale optic nerve head; one eye first; systemic: malaise, weight loss, fever, temporal/occipital headache, scalp tenderness (hair combing), jaw claudication (pain with chewing)
fields.diagnosis: ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and CRP (C-reactive protein); temporal artery biopsy is the gold standard (may wait up to 1 week after starting steroids); color Doppler ultrasound may be suggestive
fields.treatment: Refer emergently any patient over 50 with sudden vision loss; early IV (intravenous) methylprednisolone x3 days, then slow oral taper for 6–12+ months; famotidine for ulcer prophylaxis; tocilizumab as steroid-sparing option; osteoporosis prevention

fields.name: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (also: pseudotumor cerebri)
fields.definition: Elevated intracranial pressure (elevated lumbar puncture opening pressure) of idiopathic cause; also called pseudotumor cerebri.
fields.etiology: Idiopathic.
fields.risk_factors: Overweight; obesity-related metabolic syndrome is often associated.
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Intractable headaches of variable features · transient visual loss · pulsatile tinnitus (intracranial noises) · pain behind the eyes · mild pain with eye movement or globe compression · signs: [[★ papilledema]], visual field loss, abducens (sixth cranial nerve) palsy.
fields.diagnosis: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of brain with and without contrast plus magnetic resonance venography (rules out cerebral venous sinus thrombosis) · lumbar puncture: elevated opening pressure · systemic blood pressure · ophthalmology: perimetry, dilated fundoscopy, optic nerve photography.
fields.treatment: Start acetazolamide promptly + weight reduction program with a dietitian; followed by ophthalmology and neurology · failure/intolerance of medical therapy: surgical cerebrospinal fluid diversion (optic nerve sheath fenestration or ventriculoperitoneal shunt).

fields.name: Primary open-angle glaucoma
fields.definition: The most common form of glaucoma: progressive optic nerve damage and visual field loss, typically with normal (open) anterior chamber angles and elevated intraocular pressure.
fields.etiology: Optic nerve damage from elevated intraocular pressure; "primary" = no known secondary cause of open-angle glaucoma.
fields.epidemiology: Adult onset; many patients do not know they have it.
fields.risk_factors: Elevated intraocular pressure · age · race · family history of glaucoma.
fields.pathology: Open angle at the trabecular meshwork (versus closed in angle-closure) · excavation (cupping) of the optic nerve: cup-to-disc ratio 0.2 normal, 0.7 to 0.99 in glaucoma.
fields.clinical: Often asymptomatic at onset, then slowly progressive, painless vision loss · peripheral loss with [[★ central acuity initially spared]] · optic cupping, characteristic field loss on perimetry, may have elevated intraocular pressure.
fields.diagnosis: Annual ophthalmology exam · optic nerve damage on fundoscopy and/or perimetry, adult onset, normal-appearing angles on gonioscopy, no secondary cause.
fields.treatment: Goal: preserve vision · eyedrops that lower pressure by reducing aqueous production or increasing outflow: beta blockers (timolol), alpha-2 agonists (brimonidine), carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (dorzolamide), prostaglandin analogs (latanoprost) · laser trabeculoplasty · surgery · damage is irreversible, but treatment preserves vision.

fields.name: Age-related macular degeneration (also: dry (nonexudative) and wet (exudative))
fields.definition: Degeneration of the central retina (macula), in a dry (nonexudative) and a wet (exudative) form; dry can become wet.
fields.etiology: Exact cause unknown; multifactorial.
fields.pathology: Dry: soft and hard drusen, pigment clumping, geographic atrophy (waste products collect under the macula) · wet: choroidal neovascularization grows behind the retina and bleeds into it, then forms a disciform scar.
fields.clinical: Blurred vision · central scotoma · metamorphopsia (visual distortion) · wet: swelling, bleeding, scarring with rapid vision change and central vision loss; lens stays clear.
fields.diagnosis: Dry: Amsler grid for home monitoring + serial slit lamp exams · wet: the same plus fluorescein angiography and optical coherence tomography.
fields.treatment: [[★ STOP SMOKING]] · dry: AREDS2 (Age-Related Eye Disease Study 2) formula: high-dose vitamins C and E, zinc, copper, lutein, zeaxanthin (no beta carotene: lung cancer risk in smokers) · wet: intravitreal anti-VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor) injection, thermal laser photocoagulation, photodynamic therapy · slows but does not reverse loss.

fields.name: Myopia (also: nearsightedness)
fields.definition: Refractive error with excessive refractive power: distant objects focus in front of the retina.
fields.etiology: "Long eyeball", generally from an overly protruding cornea.
fields.risk_factors: Family history (genetic) · prolonged periods of reading · ocular trauma displacing the lens forward.
fields.pathology: Excess refractive power places the focal point anterior to the retina.
fields.clinical: Reduced clarity of distance vision (refractive error is the most common cause of reduced visual acuity); blur improves with corrective lenses.
fields.diagnosis: Snellen chart in primary care · pinhole occluder overcomes most refractive errors · confirmed by an optometrist with a phoropter.
fields.treatment: Refer suspected isolated refractive error to an optometrist · concave spherical lens (negative diopter) scatters light and moves focus back onto the retina · first line: spectacles, contact lenses, laser refractive surgery.

fields.name: Hyperopia (also: farsightedness)
fields.definition: Refractive error with insufficient refractive power: distant objects focus behind the retina.
fields.etiology: "Short eyeball", generally from a flat cornea.
fields.risk_factors: Anything that shortens the eye's axial length: ocular trauma displacing the lens backward, mass effect of an orbital tumor behind the retina.
fields.pathology: Insufficient refractive power places the focal point posterior to the retina.
fields.clinical: Reduced clarity of vision (refractive error is the most common cause of reduced visual acuity); blur improves with corrective lenses.
fields.diagnosis: Snellen chart in primary care · pinhole occluder overcomes most refractive errors · confirmed by an optometrist with a phoropter.
fields.treatment: Refer suspected isolated refractive error to an optometrist · convex spherical lens (positive diopter) converges light and moves focus forward onto the retina · first line: spectacles, contact lenses, laser refractive surgery.

fields.name: Astigmatism
fields.definition: Refractive error with uneven curvature of the cornea or lens, so no point focus forms on the retina: multiple focal points.
fields.etiology: Uneven (oval) curvature of the cornea or lens.
fields.risk_factors: Largely unknown; possibly genetic or developmental.
fields.pathology: Oval-shaped cornea produces multiple focal points instead of one.
fields.clinical: Blurry image; blur improves with corrective lenses.
fields.diagnosis: Snellen chart in primary care · pinhole occluder overcomes most refractive errors · confirmed by an optometrist with a phoropter.
fields.treatment: Refer suspected isolated refractive error to an optometrist · corrected with a toric lens · first line: spectacles, contact lenses, laser refractive surgery.

fields.name: Presbyopia
fields.definition: Not a refractive error: age-related loss of the lens's normal accommodation for near vision.
fields.etiology: With age the lens grows larger, thicker and much less elastic, so it can no longer round up when the zonular fibers loosen.
fields.epidemiology: Starts around age 45; essentially zero accommodation by age 65 to 70.
fields.pathology: Lost ability to increase focusing power at reading distance, so the near image focuses behind the retina.
fields.clinical: Cannot focus on objects at arm's length or closer.
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Convex lens for near only: a half-glass, or the bottom part of bifocals if distance correction is also needed.

fields.name: Strabismus
fields.definition: Misalignment of the eyes: esotropia (in), exotropia (out), hypertropia (up), hypotropia (down).
fields.etiology: Many causes: disorder of the brain, cranial nerves, neuromuscular junction or extraocular muscles · children: congenital (infantile esotropia, Duane, Mobius, Brown syndromes) or acquired (accommodative esotropia, sensory esotropia from cataract, tumors, thyroid eye disease, myasthenia gravis, raised intracranial pressure).
fields.risk_factors: Down syndrome (higher prevalence of esotropia) · cerebral palsy · thyroid eye disease (restrictive, muscle inflammation).
fields.pathology: Neurologic causes include cranial nerve palsies: third (ptosis, pupil involvement, exotropia with vertical deviation), fourth (vertical diplopia worse on downgaze), sixth (horizontal diplopia, esotropia).
fields.clinical: Adult: diplopia that disappears when either eye is covered · one eye fails to track, fixate or move fully in a gaze direction · complications: amblyopia (up to 50% of younger children), diplopia (acquired, age 4+), extraocular muscle contracture.
fields.diagnosis: History, pattern of misalignment, associated findings · confirm with the cover test (elicits fixation movement of the misaligned eye) · displaced corneal light reflex in moderate to large deviations.
fields.treatment: Refer to ophthalmology at any age for comprehensive exam; prognosis depends on the underlying cause.

fields.name: Amblyopia (also: lazy eye)
fields.definition: Developmental vision disorder: one eye fails to reach normal acuity even with glasses or contact lenses.
fields.etiology: Abnormal early visual development; the brain favors one eye · causes: strabismus (most common), anisometropia (large prescription difference between eyes; seen with eyelid hemangioma, congenital ptosis), deprivation (cataract, ptosis, corneal opacity).
fields.epidemiology: [[★ The most common cause of vision loss in children]]; up to 3 to 5% of children.
fields.risk_factors: Strabismus (up to 50% of younger children with strabismus develop amblyopia) · significant refractive difference between eyes · congenital ptosis, cataract.
fields.pathology: Brain ignores input from the weaker eye, which develops poor vision; unequal vision develops in the first decade.
fields.clinical: Usually the same signs as strabismus · unequal vision between the eyes · occlusion objection: child unbothered when the amblyopic eye is covered, fussy when the good eye is covered.
fields.diagnosis: Screen all children under 5 (USPSTF (US Preventive Services Task Force), American Academy of Pediatrics) · preverbal: fixation reflex, occlusion objection, vertical prism tests · verbal (usually over 3): optotypes; unilateral = 2 or more lines difference.
fields.treatment: Refer all to ophthalmology · patch the good eye (or dilate it with atropine drops) · outcome good for most if treated before age 7, though many do not reach normal vision; better if started under age 5, with better baseline acuity and good compliance.

fields.name: Cataract (also: acquired and pediatric (congenital))
fields.definition: Lens proteins break down and clump, clouding the lens and impairing vision; most develop slowly and are age-related.
fields.etiology: Aging (most common overall) · secondary to other eye disease · trauma · medications · systemic disease · pediatric: most commonly idiopathic.
fields.epidemiology: Mostly age-related · posterior subcapsular: [[★ more rapid onset, classically under 50]].
fields.risk_factors: Diabetes · corticosteroid use · cigarette smoking · UV (ultraviolet) exposure.
fields.pathology: Acquired: nuclear (central yellow-brown), posterior subcapsular (plaque near back of lens), cortical (peripheral spoke-like) · pediatric: [[★ zonular is the most common]], polar, nuclear, posterior lenticonus.
fields.clinical: Slowly progressive blur, glare (bright sun, night headlights) · nuclear: myopic shift, distance worse than near · posterior subcapsular: trouble reading · pediatric: inattentive if bilateral, smaller eye, nystagmus · [[★ a cataract alone does NOT cause a relative afferent pupillary defect]].
fields.diagnosis: Early: slit lamp exam · advanced: loss of red reflex on ophthalmoscopy, leukocoria (white pupil) · non-urgent ophthalmology referral for slit lamp and dilated fundoscopy (urgent if secondary uveitis or glaucoma).
fields.treatment: Surgery only (extraction with lens implant), deferred until it impairs daily activities unless neonatal (amblyopia risk) or it hinders or causes other eye disease · full visual recovery in 99% · declines surgery: trial of mydriasis (cyclopentolate), annual review · posterior capsule opacification after surgery: YAG (yttrium aluminum garnet) laser.

fields.name: Retinoblastoma
fields.definition: Rare eye cancer, primarily of young children, developing in the retina.
fields.etiology: Caused by a mutation.
fields.epidemiology: Primarily young children; rare in adults.
fields.pathology: Unilateral or bilateral retinal tumor; calcifications on imaging; metastasis usually within 1 year of diagnosis.
fields.clinical: Poor vision or strabismus · [[★ leukocoria]] if the tumor is large and near the back of the lens · smaller tumors seen only on ophthalmoscopy.
fields.diagnosis: Screen red reflex and alignment; refer suspected cases within weeks (family history: within the first 8 weeks of life, exam under anesthesia) · dilated ophthalmoscopy + imaging · biopsy contraindicated (tumor seeding).
fields.treatment: Ocular oncologist: multimodal therapy, or enucleation if very large · genetic counseling · best outcomes with early diagnosis, small tumors, no metastasis.
fields.mortality: Death nearly 100% if untreated; treated 5-year survival over 95%; no recurrence 5 years after diagnosis = cured.

fields.name: Primary uveal melanoma (also: includes iris, ciliary body and choroidal melanoma)
fields.definition: [[★ The most common eye cancer in adults]], arising from melanocytes of the uveal tract (choroid, ciliary body or iris).
fields.etiology: Melanocytes of the uvea; distinct from cutaneous and conjunctival melanoma.
fields.risk_factors: Cutaneous or iris nevi · cutaneous freckles · ocular melanocytosis.
fields.pathology: Melanotic or amelanotic; iris (anterior uvea), ciliary body or choroid (posterior uvea); ciliary body tumors may show a sentinel vessel and extrascleral extension.
fields.clinical: Usually asymptomatic, found on routine surveillance · iris melanoma: slow-growing dark brown or translucent mass, usually inferior, unilateral, over 3 mm base and 1 mm deep, prominent feeder vessel, corectopia (pupil pulled out of shape).
fields.diagnosis: Refer to ophthalmology for fundoscopy and testing (ocular oncologist) · clinical diagnosis: history, exam, imaging · FNA (fine needle aspiration) biopsy for molecular prognostic testing · differential: iris nevus, congenital heterochromia.
fields.treatment: Most common treatment: radiation therapy; surgical resection now less common; local treatment effective.
fields.mortality: High metastatic risk, often present at diagnosis; [[★ liver is the most common site]] · 10-year mortality 32%; iris melanoma far better (about 4 to 10%).

fields.name: Iris nevus (also: nevus of the iris)
fields.definition: Small, pigmented, benign spot on the iris; typically harmless.
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Pigmented or nonpigmented; typically does not grow; usually not vascular; low risk of transformation to melanoma.
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic · usually inferior half of iris · flat or minimally elevated (under 1 mm), uncommonly over 3 mm · may cause corectopia (pupil pulled out of shape) or iris ectropion (iris pigment epithelium on the anterior iris surface).
fields.diagnosis: Refer to ophthalmology to rule out melanoma · ABCDEF growth predictors: Age 40 or under, Blood in anterior chamber, Clock-hour inferior, Diffuse, Ectropion, Feathery margins.
fields.treatment: Ophthalmology surveillance, more frequent at first, then annual with dilated fundoscopy · ocular oncologist for concerning lesions.

fields.name: Conjunctival melanoma
fields.definition: Rare but potentially fatal eye cancer of the conjunctiva.
fields.etiology: More similar to cutaneous and mucosal melanoma than to uveal melanoma.
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Usually asymptomatic, found on routine surveillance · nodular, well-vascularized, dark brown or translucent conjunctival mass · prominent conjunctival feeder vessel.
fields.diagnosis: Refer to ophthalmology (ocular oncologist) · clinical diagnosis: history, exam, imaging · wide excisional biopsy · differential: conjunctival nevus (stable, cysts, well-defined borders), primary acquired melanosis.
fields.treatment: Wide excision (orbital exenteration if advanced) + adjunctive radiation · sentinel lymph node biopsy to detect early metastasis.

fields.name: Squamous cell carcinoma
fields.definition: Not covered in the lecture
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Non-pigmented lesion that may appear gelatinous or leukoplakic (white patch).
fields.diagnosis: Can be mistaken for amelanotic melanoma.
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture
