fields.name: Open globe injury
fields.definition: Ocular injury with a full-thickness defect in the cornea and/or sclera; divided into full-thickness eye wall laceration and globe rupture
fields.etiology: Sharp object or high-velocity projectile (eye wall laceration) or severe blunt trauma (globe rupture)
fields.pathology: Intraocular compartments are exposed to the external environment
fields.clinical: Pupil distorted (usually toward the wound); flat anterior chamber; extruding uveal tissue; massive hemorrhagic chemosis; soft eye; deep eyelid laceration; intraocular blood (hyphema, vitreous hemorrhage)
fields.diagnosis: CT (computed tomography) without contrast for eye penetration; with metal or organic penetration: CT of the orbit, no MRI (magnetic resonance imaging); never dilate the eye when trauma is suspected
fields.treatment: Tape a protective shield over the eye and consult ophthalmology immediately; antiemetic, analgesics, tetanus vaccine; do not remove a penetrating object; immediate surgical repair

fields.name: Full-thickness eye wall laceration
fields.definition: Open globe injury that cuts completely through the cornea, sclera, or both
fields.etiology: Sharp object or high-velocity projectile (e.g., fishing hook, knife)
fields.pathology: Object may be withdrawn/extruded before evaluation, retained in the wound, or pass through (entry and exit wound); cut lens capsule makes the lens hydrated, edematous, opaque; lens fragments in the anterior chamber cause inflammation
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Fundoscopic exam, always checking the anterior compartments
fields.treatment: Lensectomy required but may be delayed past globe repair (to treat hyphema/inflammation and plan intraocular lens placement); leave posterior-segment foreign bodies alone at initial evaluation

fields.name: Globe rupture
fields.definition: Splitting or tearing of the cornea and/or sclera at a weak point
fields.etiology: Severe blunt ocular trauma (e.g., car airbag, fist, baseball)
fields.pathology: Common sites: posterior to the extraocular muscles (especially superonasal quadrant), along prior intraocular surgery incisions, lamina cribrosa
fields.clinical: Suspect with any blunt trauma causing massive hemorrhagic chemosis or a soft eye
fields.diagnosis: CT (computed tomography) may be done to rule out a foreign object
fields.treatment: Protective shield taped over the eye and immediate ophthalmology consult; antiemetic, analgesics, tetanus vaccine; immediate surgical repair (wound exploration and repair)

fields.name: Corneal abrasion
fields.definition: Scratching or scraping away of some of the corneal epithelium
fields.etiology: Injury such as a fingernail or contact lens manipulation
fields.epidemiology: One of the most common ophthalmic injuries
fields.pathology: Loss of epithelium exposes the basement membrane, which takes up fluorescein
fields.clinical: Severe foreign body sensation, tearing, light sensitivity, blurred vision
fields.diagnosis: Slit-lamp exam with fluorescein (stains the exposed basement membrane) shows the extent
fields.treatment: Topical broad-spectrum antibacterial: erythromycin ointment (no contact lens, or organic source); ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin or tobramycin (contact lens wear); patching may ease pain; periodic re-exam; never prescribe topical anesthetic drops (delay healing, mask worsening, cause corneal ulcer)

fields.name: Corneal/conjunctival foreign body
fields.definition: Object with too little momentum to pass through the eye wall becomes embedded in the cornea or conjunctiva
fields.etiology: History of grinding or striking metal
fields.pathology: Iron or copper foreign bodies leave a rust ring
fields.clinical: Foreign body sensation, light sensitivity, excessive tearing
fields.diagnosis: Slit lamp shows small bodies; larger ones visible on diffuse light exam; linear vertical corneal epithelial defects mean a foreign body under the upper lid (tarsal conjunctiva): evert the lid promptly
fields.treatment: Topical anesthetic, slit-lamp exam, remove with sterile 27-gauge needle (upper-lid body: cotton-tipped applicator); rust ring: battery-operated burr drill; antibiotics + abrasion care; ophthalmology if it may have passed through the cornea

fields.name: Hyphema
fields.definition: Hemorrhage/blood in the anterior chamber from trauma injuring its blood vessels
fields.etiology: Blunt or penetrating trauma
fields.risk_factors: Sickle cell anemia and aspirin/antiplatelet drugs raise the risk of secondary hemorrhage
fields.pathology: High risk of secondary hemorrhage causing permanent visual loss; most rebleeding occurs in the first 72 hours
fields.clinical: Blurred vision, eye pain, light sensitivity; can be a sign of open globe
fields.diagnosis: Diffuse light exam (gross hyphema), slit lamp, comprehensive ophthalmic exam; measure IOP (intraocular pressure) unless penetrating injury is suspected
fields.treatment: Goal: prevent rebleeding; bedrest, head of bed slightly up; antiemetics; corticosteroids; cycloplegic drops; oral aminocaproic acid (antifibrinolytic); avoid aspirin/antiplatelets; treat high pressure (beta blockers, pilocarpine, acetazolamide, osmotic agents)

fields.name: Lid laceration (also: eyelid laceration)
fields.definition: Laceration of the eyelid; full-thickness or partial-thickness
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Unrepaired deep medial-third laceration (canalicular system transection) causes chronic tearing
fields.clinical: Full-thickness lid laceration accompanies corneal laceration or globe rupture in about 2/3 of cases
fields.diagnosis: Determine whether it goes through the tarsal plate of the upper lid; check margin, medial canthus, lacrimal system, inner lid surface, ptosis, levator
fields.treatment: Ophthalmology consult: lid margin, within 6-8 mm of medial canthus, lacrimal duct/sac, inner lid surface, ptosis, tarsal plate or levator; partial-thickness: emergency room repair, ophthalmology in 2-3 days; face may be left open 24 h before closure

fields.name: Orbital and lid contusion
fields.definition: Eye trauma causing soft tissue swelling within the orbit without hemorrhage
fields.etiology: Eye trauma
fields.pathology: Tarsal plate and orbital septal margin act as a wall that keeps blood in the anterior tissues
fields.clinical: Preseptal ecchymosis or hematoma
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Supportive to surgical depending on status; must rule out brain trauma

fields.name: Periorbital hematoma
fields.definition: Bleeding within the orbit, around the eye
fields.etiology: Trauma; orbit/eyelid surgery; peribulbar injections; orbital varices; lymphangiomas and arteriovenous malformations; anticoagulants; sickle cell anemia; orbital pseudotumor; idiopathic
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Lateral canthotomy with cantholysis (expose lateral canthal tendon, incise its inferior branch) to drain the blood

fields.name: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
fields.definition: Retinal detachment from one or more full-thickness breaks in the sensory retina
fields.etiology: Retinal breaks + vitreous traction let liquefied vitreous pass into the subretinal space; usually spontaneous and age-related
fields.risk_factors: Myopia, cataract surgery, ocular trauma; usually preceded by posterior vitreous detachment
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Shadow or curtain descending over vision; cloudy/smoky vision, floaters, flashes; monocular field defects; reduced central acuity if macula involved
fields.diagnosis: History and dilated eye exam; refer immediately, seen by ophthalmology within 24 hours
fields.treatment: Surgical; immediate ophthalmology; pain control, antiemetics, head of bed at 30-40 degrees

fields.name: Traction retinal detachment
fields.definition: One of the three types of retinal detachment; typically more localized, with a concave shape
fields.etiology: Most commonly proliferative diabetic retinopathy
fields.pathology: More localized, concave detachment; starts along the vasculature, then spreads to the retina and macula
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Surgical

fields.name: Exudative (serous) retinal detachment (also: serous retinal detachment)
fields.definition: Detachment without a retinal break or vitreoretinal traction
fields.etiology: Systemic vascular or inflammatory disease, or intraocular tumors
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Manage the underlying condition

fields.name: Orbital floor (blowout) fracture (also: blowout fracture; orbital fracture)
fields.definition: Fracture of the orbital floor (most often) or medial wall
fields.etiology: Blunt object (fist, ball) raises orbital pressure and blows out the floor; or a blow to the infraorbital rim buckles the floor
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Periorbital ecchymosis, lid edema, infraorbital numbness, subcutaneous emphysema; diplopia on upward gaze (inferior rectus entrapment) or lateral gaze (medial rectus); severe pain, bradycardia, vomiting on attempted eye movement (entrapment); children: white-eyed blowout (entrapment without orbital soft tissue signs)
fields.diagnosis: CT (computed tomography) of orbits and midface
fields.treatment: No entrapment/eye injury: ice, analgesics, follow up 2-3 days; sinus blood: antibiotics; true blowout: ophthalmology (30% globe injury); entrapment: immediate facial trauma surgeon (muscle necrosis); surgery may wait 1-2 weeks

fields.name: Basilar skull fracture
fields.definition: Linear fracture of the skull base (cribriform, orbital plate of frontal, temporal, sphenoid or occipital bone)
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Often asymptomatic; Battle sign (bruising behind the ear), raccoon eyes (periorbital bruising); hemotympanum (blood in the middle ear); CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) leak: clear or pink rhinorrhea, otorrhea
fields.diagnosis: CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) may be dextrose-positive; halo/double ring sign (inner ring of blood, outer ring of cerebrospinal fluid) on filter paper or bedsheet; CT (computed tomography) of orbits, though fractures may not show
fields.treatment: CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) leak: neurosurgery consult and admission; admission based on condition, associated injuries, brain injury on CT (computed tomography); antibiotics controversial (resistant organisms)
